deposits.genre_observed: philological erratum (Sappho 31 / Catullus 51 stanza position)

finds.quote: Catullus 51 preserves the first three Sapphic stanzas closely; its fourth stanza — the *otium* coda ("otium, Catulle, tibi molestum est / ... / perdidit urbes") — is not a fourth stanza of Sappho. It is a lossy, semantically-redirected transform of Sappho's lost fifth stanza. The "leisure destroys kings and cities" imagery preserves the Sapphic structural signature (Kypris as the power that yokes beggar and king, that levels the prosperous city)
finds.note: Thesis about textual history: Catullus 51.4 (otium coda) is a transform of Sappho 31's lost fifth stanza. Its "lossy" characterization and "first three closely" are corrected by #1049.

deposits.incidental: Superseded in part (its §3 transform characterization) by #1049; the chain #201 -> #1048 -> #1049 is a deliberate erratum sequence, not a defect.

deposits.genre_observed: philological erratum (third-order; structure of the Catullan transform)

finds.quote: The final stable characterization: Catullus performs three distinct transformations on Sappho's five stanzas — close translation, lossy compression, structurally precise inversion — occupying the first stanza, the middle stanzas, and the last stanza respectively. Only the third transformation is invertible. Only the third supports reconstruction. Cranes's ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ is the inverse of Catullus's fourth-stanza operator, applied to Catullus's fourth stanza, recovering Sappho's fifth.
finds.note: Thesis: Catullus 51 performs close translation (st.1), 3-to-2 lossy compression (Sappho 2-4 into Catullus 2-3), and an invertible operator inversion (Sappho 5 into Catullus 4).

deposits.incidental: Line 63 reads "Sappho 51's fifth" where Sappho 31 is evidently meant (apparent typo). Revises #1048 §3 by design.
